live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Gallstone disease does not typically cause chronic wheat-related bloating and diarrhoea. B. Pancreatitis causes acute upper abdominal pain and systemic illness. D. Diverticulitis causes acute abdominal pain and systemic inflammatory features. E. Appendicitis causes an acute surgical presentation.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Coeliac serology is only reliable while gluten is being eaten; anyone who has already cut it out should reintroduce gluten for several weeks before testing.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Chronic bloating and diarrhoea ↓ improvement on avoiding wheat ↓ gluten-related disease suspected ↓ test before any diet change ↓ coeliac disease
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, diverticulitis — a common cause of bowel symptoms in adults, but it causes acute pain and fever, not chronic wheat-linked bloating.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Test for coeliac disease before, not after, starting a gluten-free diet.

live_plab_copy.stem: A 41-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of upper abdominal discomfort after meals. The pain is particularly associated with fatty food and lasts several hours. Which diagnosis should be considered?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Episodic upper abdominal pain after meals, particularly fatty meals, is typical of biliary colic from gallstone disease.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Renal colic is typically severe flank pain radiating towards the groin. B. IBS causes recurrent abdominal pain associated with bowel habit changes. D. Cystitis causes urinary symptoms. E. Appendicitis usually develops into right lower quadrant pain.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Episodic upper abdominal/right upper quadrant pain triggered by fatty meals and lasting several hours, without fever, is typical of biliary colic from gallstones.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Use the fatty-food trigger and episodic, self-limiting nature of the pain to point to gallstone disease, distinguishing it from appendicitis, renal colic, or IBS.
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: Renal colic is a plausible distractor for severe abdominal pain, but its classic radiation (flank to groin) is different from the postprandial epigastric/right upper quadrant pattern here.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Postprandial pain after fatty food = biliary colic.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A 30-year-old woman develops recurrent abdominal bloating and diarrhoea after consuming foods containing wheat. She is considering starting a gluten-free diet before seeing her doctor.

What is important if coeliac disease is suspected?

options.A: Start a gluten-free diet now to see if symptoms settle
options.B: Continue eating gluten until coeliac testing is done
options.C: Exclude dairy as well as gluten before testing
options.D: Take a course of antibiotics for bacterial overgrowth
options.E: Request a stool culture before any dietary change

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: B. Continue eating gluten until coeliac testing is done
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Starting a gluten-free diet before testing can affect the accuracy of coeliac investigations.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Starting a gluten-free diet before testing reduces the accuracy of coeliac investigations. C. Dairy exclusion is not required and does not aid coeliac testing. D. There is no evidence of bacterial overgrowth, and antibiotics do not treat coeliac disease. E. Stool culture does not investigate coeliac disease.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Coeliac serology and biopsy depend on gluten exposure, so patients should keep eating gluten in more than one meal every day for several weeks before testing.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Wheat-related bloating and diarrhoea ↓ Suspected coeliac disease ↓ Tests rely on ongoing gluten exposure ↓ Continue eating gluten until testing is done
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, start a gluten-free diet now — symptom relief seems a quick answer, but it can make serology and biopsy falsely negative and delay diagnosis.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Keep eating gluten until coeliac testing is complete.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Coeliac disease means gluten: wheat, barley and rye.

A patient with rectal inflammation reports repeatedly feeling that they need to open their bowels even after passing stool.

What is this symptom called?

live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Haematemesis means vomiting blood. B. Melena describes black, tarry stools. C. Steatorrhoea describes fatty stools. D. Dysphagia means difficulty swallowing.

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, steatorrhoea — another bowel symptom term, but it describes fatty stool, not the feeling of incomplete evacuation.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Persistent urge to defecate despite emptying is tenesmus, a rectal symptom.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Urgency means cannot defer defecation; tenesmus means feeling incompletely emptied.

options.D: IBS raises cancer risk after 10 years of symptoms

live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. IBS does not increase colorectal cancer risk. C. Chemotherapy is not a treatment for IBS. D. Symptom duration in IBS does not confer cancer risk. E. It is not regarded as a premalignant disease.

live_plab_copy.thinking: Established IBS ↓ Functional gut disorder without structural damage ↓ Not premalignant ↓ IBS does not itself increase colorectal cancer risk
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, IBS raises cancer risk after 10 years — it echoes the rule for long-standing inflammatory bowel disease, but that applies to colitis, not functional IBS.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: IBS is not premalignant; do not confuse it with inflammatory bowel disease.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Raised ALP and GGT together point to cholestasis.

akt_source.stem: A 48-year-old man develops severe epigastric pain after heavy alcohol consumption. CT confirms acute pancreatitis. Which complication can occur as a result of pancreatic enzyme-mediated fat necrosis?
akt_source.why_correct: Fat necrosis can bind calcium in areas of pancreatic inflammation, causing hypocalcaemia in severe pancreatitis.
akt_source.why_wrong: A. Pancreatitis does not cause polycythaemia through this mechanism. B. Thyroid function is unrelated to pancreatic fat necrosis. C. Hyperkalaemia is not caused directly by pancreatic fat necrosis. E. Hypernatraemia is not a characteristic complication of pancreatitis.

live_plab_copy.stem: A 55-year-old man presents with severe epigastric pain and is found to have acute pancreatitis. His calcium concentration is low. Which mechanism can contribute to hypocalcaemia in acute pancreatitis?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Pancreatic fat necrosis can release fatty acids that bind calcium, contributing to hypocalcaemia.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Aldosterone primarily regulates sodium and potassium. C. This is not the mechanism responsible for hypocalcaemia in pancreatitis. D. Increased PTH would generally increase serum calcium. E. Increased calcium absorption would tend to increase rather than decrease serum calcium.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Hypocalcaemia in acute pancreatitis results partly from saponification, where fatty acids released by fat necrosis bind calcium; low calcium is a marker of severe disease.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Acute pancreatitis ↓ released lipase digests surrounding fat ↓ fat necrosis releases fatty acids ↓ fatty acids bind calcium (saponification) ↓ hypocalcaemia
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, excess PTH secretion — sounds like a calcium-related mechanism, but raised PTH would increase serum calcium, not lower it.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Pancreatitis lowers calcium through fat necrosis and saponification.
